# BGPsec: Architectural Vision and Practical Reality

BGPsec signs the AS path. RPKI and ASPA do not. This chapter is what that signature promises, what it costs, and why production edges in 2026 secure paths with filters, roles, and ASPA records instead of BGPsec.

## Learning goals

- State the attack BGPsec is designed to close
- Describe a signed path as a chain of hop signatures under router certificates
- Contrast that guarantee with ROV and with ASPA
- Explain the deployment barriers without treating them as a reason to skip origin validation

## The BGPsec Problem Statement: Securing the AS Path

Chapter 3's path edits (shortening, splicing, inserting a victim AS) all work because AS_PATH is a list the neighbour writes. ROV checks the rightmost AS against a ROA and stops. ASPA checks whether the shape of the list matches signed provider sets and stops. Neither check proves that the AS in position *n* actually handed the route to the AS in position *n+1*.

BGPsec (RFC 8205) is aimed at that gap. A receiving network should be able to reject a path whose signatures do not chain from the origin to the neighbour. An attacker who is not on the path and who does not hold a router key for an AS in the path should not be able to splice themselves in or delete a hop.

The problem statement does not include leaks by a network that is legitimately on the path and signs the export. A signed leak is still a leak. Export policy remains mandatory.

## BGPsec Protocol: Signed Path Attributes and Key Hierarchies

BGPsec replaces the bare AS_PATH, on sessions that negotiate it, with a signed attribute. Each hop signs the prefix, the AS it is sending to, and the signature it received. The signature covers the intended receiver so a signed update cannot be replayed to a different neighbour. Validation walks the signatures back to the origin and checks that each signing key belongs to the AS that supposedly signed.

Keys come from the RPKI. BGPsec router certificates bind a router key to an AS number (RFC 8209). The algorithm profile is separate (RFC 8208) so the suite can change. Relying parties that support these certificates can hand router keys to routers over RTR version 1. The router still does the per-path cryptography. That is a different cost model from ROV, where the router only stores VRPs and compares prefixes.

Two operational consequences follow. First, every AS on a path must sign or the path is not BGPsec-valid end to end. Second, the CPU cost sits on the routers during update processing, which is the opposite of the RPKI design that kept cryptography off the forwarding engines.

## BGPsec vs RPKI/ROV: Different Guarantees, Different Trade-offs

| Control | Guarantees | Does not guarantee | Where the work runs |
|---------|------------|--------------------|---------------------|
| ROV | Origin AS and length match a ROA | Path, neighbour, or leak status | Validator does cryptography. Router compares triples |
| ASPA | Path shape matches signed provider lists, where objects exist | Each hop actually forwarded the route | Validator plus a path walk on the router |
| BGPsec | Each hop signed this prefix onward to the next AS | The hop was wise to export it. Partial deployment yields unsigned paths | Per-update signatures on every BGP speaker in the path |
| Prefix filters | This neighbour is allowed to send this prefix | Anything about the rest of the Internet | Your generator and your edge |

Partial BGPsec is a different protocol behaviour from partial ROV. A route can be ROV Valid for the origin and unsigned in BGPsec. Policy has to accept unsigned paths for as long as most of the Internet does not sign, which removes the reason to pay for signatures. ROV's NotFound analogue is the entire path. That is why origin validation could deploy incrementally and path signatures have not.

## Operational Barriers to BGPsec Adoption

The barriers are engineering, not awareness.

- **Incremental deployment.** The first two networks to sign gain nothing on paths that leave their little island and re-enter the unsigned Internet
- **Router cost.** Signature verification on a full-table session is a control-plane budget. ROV was accepted because it avoided that budget
- **Key operations.** Router certificates, rollover, and "this route server signs on behalf of members" are new failure modes on every speaker
- **Feature support.** Open-source implementations have had pieces of signing and validation for years, often incomplete and sometimes behind the current RFC. Commercial defaults do not wait on BGPsec the way they now wait on RTR
- **Interaction with existing tools.** Route reflection, confederations, AS-path prepending as traffic engineering, and route servers all have to be specified in the signature design or they break. Each one was a multi-year argument
- **A cheaper partial answer arrived.** ASPA and RFC 9234 give operators something to deploy against leaks without per-update signatures

None of these barriers make path forgery acceptable. They explain why the mitigation you will actually configure is "do not take a full table from a customer" plus origin validation.

## BGPsec Deployment Status and Pilot Networks

BGPsec is a published standard (RFC 8205 and the companion certificate and algorithm RFCs). It is not a feature of the default-free zone. Public pilots and research testbeds have shown small topologies in which two or three implementations exchange signed updates. SIDN Labs' 2025 survey of open-source speakers found signing and validation scattered across FRR, BIRD, GoBGP-related stacks, and research forks, with gaps in cache integration and in mutual interoperability. That is a pilot landscape.

Do not write a production acceptance policy that requires BGPsec-valid paths. You will drop the Internet. Do allow a lab inside this book's Containerlab path to experiment, on private ASNs, with a local RPKI, if a later writing pass adds that lab. Until that lab exists, this chapter is the specification and the deployment reality, not a configuration guide.

## BGPsec as a Long-Term Goal vs Short-Term Tool

Keep the goal. A fully signed AS path is the statement BGP never had. Spend the current budget on the controls that change forwarding this quarter:

1. Tight ROAs for your own space, and AS0 ROAs for space you do not announce
2. Drop RPKI Invalid on transit and peer sessions
3. Customer and peer prefix filters generated from the contract, IRR, and ROAs
4. Max-prefix and session authentication or GTSM
5. ASPA records published for your AS, and OTC or BGP roles where the OS supports them
6. Telemetry that tells you when your prefix's origin changes anywhere it is seen

Revisit BGPsec when more than a toy fraction of your paths would validate, when the OS you run verifies signatures from a cache you already trust, and when you have a rollback that does not involve turning BGP off. Until then, BGPsec is a design you should understand so you do not buy a product that claims "path security" and only does ROV. ROV is worth buying. It is not BGPsec.

## Summary

- BGPsec signs each hop of a path to a named receiver
- The signature needs router certificates in the RPKI and cryptography on the routers
- ROV and ASPA answer cheaper questions and deploy without every AS participating
- 2026 production status is standards-plus-pilots, not enforcement
- Build origin and relationship controls now. Keep path signatures as the long-term goal
